parameters.query:
-- Claim the right to send, THEN send — and work out WHO it goes to here rather than
-- trusting the caller: a chat id passed in could address the wrong customer entirely.
-- The unique key includes recipient_ref, so a notice to a new stylist after a reassignment,
-- or to the next person a waitlist offer rolls to, is not mistaken for a duplicate.
-- Always returns exactly one row, so a fan-out of N items stays index-aligned.
WITH req AS (
  SELECT $1::bigint AS appointment_id, $2::text AS recipient, $3::text AS kind,
         $4::text AS manager_chat, $5::bigint AS waitlist_entry_id
), res AS (
  -- A waitlist offer is about one appointment but addressed to a DIFFERENT customer: the one
  -- waiting, not the one who cancelled. Naming the entry still keeps the lookup server-side —
  -- the caller never supplies a chat id.
  SELECT a.id, a.status,
         CASE r.recipient WHEN 'stylist' THEN a.stylist_id
                          WHEN 'client'  THEN COALESCE(wc.id, a.client_id)
                          ELSE 'manager' END AS recipient_ref,
         CASE r.recipient WHEN 'stylist' THEN st.telegram_chat_id
                          WHEN 'client'  THEN COALESCE(wc.channel_user_id, c.channel_user_id)
                          -- A manager alert is the salon's audit trail and must be recorded
                          -- even when no manager chat is configured to receive it.
                          ELSE COALESCE(r.manager_chat, 'manager-desk') END AS chat_id
  FROM req r
  JOIN appointment a ON a.id = r.appointment_id
  JOIN stylist st    ON st.id = a.stylist_id
  JOIN client  c     ON c.id  = a.client_id
  LEFT JOIN waitlist_entry w ON w.id = r.waitlist_entry_id
  LEFT JOIN client wc        ON wc.id = w.client_id
), ins AS (
  INSERT INTO notification_log (appointment_id, recipient, recipient_ref, kind, channel, detail)
  SELECT r.appointment_id, r.recipient, res.recipient_ref, r.kind, 'telegram', 'claimed'
  FROM req r CROSS JOIN res
  -- Never claim what cannot be delivered: an unreachable person would be marked "sent"
  -- forever. Leaving it unclaimed means the next run tries again once they have a chat id.
  WHERE res.chat_id IS NOT NULL AND btrim(res.chat_id) <> ''
    -- A reminder for an appointment cancelled between the sweep and the send must not go
    -- out. Notices ABOUT a cancellation obviously still may.
    AND (r.kind NOT IN ('booked','reminder_24h','reminder_1h') OR res.status = 'confirmed')
  ON CONFLICT (appointment_id, recipient, recipient_ref, kind) DO NOTHING
  RETURNING id
)
SELECT json_build_object(
  'found',         (SELECT count(*) FROM res) > 0,
  'status',        (SELECT status FROM res),
  'chat_id',       (SELECT chat_id FROM res),
  'recipient_ref', (SELECT recipient_ref FROM res),
  'claimed',       (SELECT count(*) FROM ins) > 0,
  'log_id',        (SELECT id FROM ins)
) AS result;

options.queryReplacement: ={{ [$json.appointment_id, $json.recipient, $json.kind, $json.manager_chat || (() => { try { return $env.MANAGER_TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID || null; } catch (e) { return null; } })(), $json.waitlist_entry_id || null] }}

parameters.content:
## 39 · send a notice, exactly once

**In** `{appointment_id, recipient, kind, text}` — one item or many.

Claims the right to send by INSERTing into `notification_log`, and only then sends. Two schedulers racing, or the same run twice, produce one winner and one silent no-op.

**Who it goes to is worked out here**, from the appointment — never taken from the caller, because a chat id passed in could address the wrong customer.

It will not claim what it cannot deliver (nobody to send to), nor a reminder for an appointment that stopped being confirmed since the sweep picked it up. If the send then fails the claim is **given back**, because a claim that never arrived would otherwise mark the notice sent forever.
